claims.text: The ball-milled Mg-Al-Ti-V-Fe-Co powder is a nanocrystalline BCC solid solution.
The ball-milled powder has a high dislocation density.
Milling can introduce surface oxides or oxygen into the powder.
Sintering at 950–1000 °C supplies enough diffusion activity to precipitate secondary phases from the supersaturated BCC matrix.
Ti, V, and Fe segregate from the Mg-Al-Ti-V-Fe-Co BCC solid solution during SPS.
The segregated elements form Ti-rich intermetallic phases such as Ti-V-rich, Ti-Fe-rich, or Laves phases.
The secondary phases form a continuous network at grain boundaries.
The Ti-rich secondary-phase network acts as a kinetic barrier to atomic diffusion.
The secondary-phase network prevents grain coarsening.
The secondary-phase network suppresses Mg loss during sintering.
The precipitated phases promote formation of a dense Cr/Ti/V-rich passive oxide film during subsequent exposure.
The optimized material will attain more than 98% theoretical density.
The optimized material will attain a Vickers hardness above 700 HV.
The optimized material will have lower oxidation and corrosion rates than samples sintered below 800 °C or above 1000 °C.
Sintering at 800 °C or below provides insufficient driving force for secondary-phase precipitation and bulk densification.
Sintering above 1000 °C causes significant Mg evaporation and composition deviation.
Mg evaporation disrupts the barrier network and produces a porous, compositionally inhomogeneous microstructure with poor mechanical and corrosion properties.
The identity of the secondary phase, specifically Laves phase versus TiO, depends on oxygen content and local Mg concentration.
Secondary-phase precipitation is interface-controlled, analogous to BCC nucleation and growth in CoCrFeNiTi.

contradictions.description: The stated alloy contains no Cr, but the mechanism predicts formation of a Cr/Ti/V-rich passive film without introducing any Cr source.
The hypothesis and structural mediator specify Ti-rich intermetallic phases, while the uncertainty field allows TiO, an oxide rather than an intermetallic, to be the secondary phase.
The processing conditions state that 1000 °C is the maximum allowed temperature, but the proposed falsification experiment requires SPS at 1050 °C.
